heroLead: Warrior sits on the Locust Fork near the Jefferson-Walker county line, deep enough into the region's coal mining history that a mineral interest here often carries more documented background than the town's small size would suggest.
intro: The town of Warrior grew up around coal mining along the Locust Fork, close enough to Walker County that its mineral history overlaps with the coal seam gas development that made that county significant to the Black Warrior Basin. Underground mining in and around Warrior went on for generations, and when coalbed methane technology matured, some of the same seams that had been mined for coal were revisited for gas.

If you hold a mineral interest connected to land near Warrior, there's a reasonable chance it carries some production history, whether from coal royalties decades ago, gas royalties more recently, or both at different points. We start by pinning down exactly what your deed covers before we talk about value.

sections.heading: A town built on layered mineral history
paragraphs: Warrior's position along the Locust Fork put it inside one of the more heavily mined corridors of northwest Jefferson County, and that mining activity shaped how land here was bought, sold, and reserved for well over a century. It's common to find deeds referencing coal rights specifically, sometimes separately from oil and gas rights that were reserved or sold at a different point entirely.

We treat these as two potentially separate questions when we review a Warrior-area interest: what coal rights, if any, you hold, and what oil and gas rights, if any, you hold, since a family can easily own one without the other.

sections.heading: Coalbed methane near the Jefferson-Walker line
paragraphs: Because Warrior sits close to the border with Walker County, some CBM units and historic degasification wells tied to underground mining extended across the county line, meaning a tract technically in Jefferson County can still be part of a unit whose other acreage sits in Walker County. We check unit boundaries directly rather than assuming based on which county your legal description names.

If your family's interest has ever been part of one of these cross-county units, that production history factors meaningfully into how we price it, and we'll pull the specific well or unit records to confirm.

sections.heading: Making sense of an older Warrior-area deed
paragraphs: Deeds tied to coal-era land in Warrior sometimes use language that doesn't match how minerals are described today, referencing specific coal seams by old company terminology or reserving rights in ways that read differently than a modern lease. We're used to interpreting this older language and matching it against the current legal description of your property.

If you inherited the interest and aren't sure exactly what was reserved or by whom, that's a normal starting point. Give us what you have, even if it's incomplete, and we'll work through the Jefferson County Probate Court records to fill in the gaps.

faqs.question: Do I own coal rights, gas rights, or both on my Warrior property?
faqs.answer: It depends on your specific deed history, since these were often severed separately in this part of the county. We review your paperwork to determine exactly what estate you hold.

faqs.question: Is my interest part of a unit that extends into Walker County?
faqs.answer: Possibly, since some historic units near Warrior cross the county line. We check current and historic unit boundaries against your legal description rather than assuming based on county alone.

faqs.question: My deed uses old coal-era terminology I don't understand. Can you help interpret it?
faqs.answer: Yes, we're familiar with how older Jefferson County coal and mineral deeds were typically written and can match that language against your property's current legal description.
